lecture.title: How memory works, and why we forget

slides.title: Encoding, storage and retrieval
bullets: Memory has three stages: encoding, storage and retrieval.
Encoding means getting information in. Attention matters most here.
Storage means keeping information over time.
Retrieval means getting information back out when you need it.
Many “I forgot” moments are retrieval failures, like a word on the tip of your tongue.

slides.title: Working memory and chunking
bullets: Working memory holds a small amount of information while you use it.
Miller (1956) suggested about 7 items. Later research suggests nearer 4 chunks. Researchers debate the exact limit.
Chunking groups items into meaningful units, like splitting a phone number into parts.
Overloading working memory makes new learning harder.

slides.title: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve (1885)
bullets: Hermann Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays.
The forgetting curve shows forgetting is fastest soon after learning, then slows down.
Relearning something is faster than learning it the first time.
The exact shape of the curve depends on the material and how well it was learned.

slides.title: The spacing effect
bullets: The spacing effect: study spread over several sessions beats the same time in one session.
It has been found across many ages, subjects and materials (Cepeda et al., 2006).
A gap lets some forgetting happen, so the next review takes more effort and lasts longer.
The best gap depends on how long you need to remember. Researchers debate the ideal schedule.

slides.title: Retrieval practice (the testing effect)
bullets: Retrieval practice means recalling information from memory, not re-reading it.
Recalling strengthens memory more than re-reading. This is called the testing effect.
Roediger and Karpicke (2006): students who practised recall remembered more a week later.
Self-quizzes, flashcards and writing on a blank page all count.
It feels harder than re-reading. That effort is part of why it works.

slides.title: Sleep and breaks in consolidation
bullets: Consolidation is the process that makes new memories more stable after learning.
Sleep after learning supports consolidation.
Losing sleep makes it harder to learn new information the next day.
Some studies suggest a short quiet rest after learning helps too. Researchers debate how large this effect is.

slides.title: Why multitasking and screen switching hurt learning
bullets: For demanding tasks, we do not truly do two things at once. We switch between them.
Each switch has a task-switching cost: extra time and more mistakes.
Sana et al. (2013): students multitasking on laptops in a lecture learned less, and so did students who could see their screens.
Phone notifications may pull attention even when ignored. Researchers debate how large this effect is.

slides.title: Practical study tips
bullets: Avoid cramming: short sessions spread over days work better.
Test yourself first, then check your notes.
Study one thing at a time. Put your phone out of reach.
Take short breaks, and protect your sleep before exams.
Chunk big topics into small, meaningful parts.

notes:
Today we are looking at how memory works, and why we forget. Psychologists usually describe memory in three stages. Encoding is getting information in. Storage is keeping it over time. Retrieval is getting it back out when you need it. Forgetting can happen at any of these stages. If you were not paying attention, the information may never have been encoded at all. And many everyday failures are failures of retrieval: the memory is there, but you cannot reach it right now. The word on the tip of your tongue is the classic example.

While you are actively thinking, you rely on working memory. This is the small mental workspace that holds information while you use it, for example while you follow a sentence or do mental arithmetic. In 1956, George Miller suggested we can hold about seven items. Later research suggests the real limit is nearer four chunks, and researchers still debate the exact number. A chunk is a meaningful unit. We remember a phone number more easily when we split it into parts. The practical point is that working memory is easy to overload, and when it is overloaded, new learning suffers.

What happens after we learn something? In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory for lists of nonsense syllables after different delays. He found that forgetting is fastest soon after learning, and then slows down. This pattern is called the forgetting curve. He also found that relearning a list was faster than learning it the first time, so even “forgotten” material leaves a trace. The exact shape of the curve depends on what is learned and how well, but the general pattern has been found many times.

The forgetting curve leads to one of the most reliable findings in learning research: the spacing effect. If you spread your study over several sessions, you remember more than if you spend the same total time in one session. A large review by Cepeda and colleagues in 2006 found this across many ages, subjects and materials. One explanation is that a gap lets some forgetting happen, so the next review takes more effort and builds a stronger memory. How long the gaps should be depends on how long you need to remember, and the ideal schedule is still debated.

A second reliable finding is retrieval practice, also called the testing effect. Recalling information from memory strengthens it more than reading it again. In a well-known study, Roediger and Karpicke in 2006 asked students to read short passages. Some re-read the passages, while others practised recalling them. After a week, the students who practised recall remembered more. Self-quizzing, flashcards and writing everything you know on a blank page all count as retrieval practice. It feels harder than re-reading, and that effort is part of why it works.

Memories also change after learning. Consolidation is the process that makes new memories more stable over time, and sleep plays an important part in it. Sleeping after learning supports later memory, and losing sleep makes it harder to take in new information the next day. Some studies suggest that a short, quiet rest straight after learning can also help, although researchers debate how large this effect is.

This brings us to multitasking. For demanding tasks, we do not really do two things at once. We switch between them, and every switch has a task-switching cost in time and mistakes. In a study by Sana and colleagues in 2013, students who multitasked on laptops during a lecture learned less. So did students sitting nearby who could see those screens. There is also evidence that notifications can pull attention even when we ignore them, although researchers debate how large that effect is.

So what should you do? Avoid cramming, and spread your study into short sessions over several days. Test yourself first, and only then check your notes. Work on one thing at a time and put your phone out of reach. Take short breaks, protect your sleep, especially before exams, and break big topics into small, meaningful chunks. None of these need special tools. They work because they match how memory works.
key_ideas: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning, so a quick review soon after a lecture saves time later.
Recalling information from memory strengthens it more than re-reading it.
Spaced sessions, sleep and one task at a time beat cramming and switching between screens.

quiz.q: Which stage of memory is about getting information back out when you need it?
quiz.why: Retrieval is getting stored information back out.

quiz.q: Remembering a long number as three short groups is an example of…
quiz.why: Chunking groups items into meaningful units so working memory holds more.

quiz.q: According to Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, when is forgetting fastest?
options: At a steady rate the whole time
quiz.why: Forgetting is steepest soon after learning, then slows.

quiz.q: You have 3 hours to revise. Which plan is likely to give the best long-term memory?
options: 1 hour on each of 3 different days
quiz.why: The spacing effect: the same time spread over sessions beats one block.

quiz.q: In Roediger and Karpicke (2006), which students remembered the most after one week?
options: Those who re-read the passage several times
Those who read it once only
quiz.why: Practising recall beat re-reading at the one-week test.

options: The process that makes new memories more stable
quiz.why: Consolidation stabilises memories after learning, and sleep supports it.

quiz.q: In Sana et al. (2013), what happened to students who could see a classmate multitasking on a laptop?
quiz.why: Nearby students who could see the screen also scored lower.

quiz.q: A friend re-reads their notes until they feel familiar. Why might this mislead them?
options: Feeling familiar is not the same as being able to recall
quiz.why: Recognising material is easier than recalling it, so re-reading can give false confidence.

offscreen_tasks.instruction: Stand up and say 5 ideas from this lecture out loud, without looking.
steps: Walk to a window or another room while you think.

offscreen_tasks.instruction: On paper, sketch the forgetting curve from memory.
steps: Label the axes: time and amount remembered.
Add what a review does to the curve.
Snap a photo if you want to keep it.

offscreen_tasks.instruction: Explain the spacing effect in 30 seconds, as if to a friend who crams.
steps: Give one example from your own week.

offscreen_tasks.instruction: Walk while you listen to a 90-second recap of this lecture.
steps: The screen dims while you're away.
When it ends, name the 3 stages of memory out loud.

offscreen_tasks.instruction: Find one thing around you that pulls your attention while you study, and move it out of sight.
steps: Think: what task-switching cost does it cause?
Notice how the space feels without it.

glossary.def: Getting information into memory. It depends on paying attention.
Getting stored information back out when you need it.
The small mental workspace that holds information while you use it.
Grouping items into meaningful units so they are easier to hold.
A graph showing forgetting is fastest soon after learning, then slows.
Study spread over several sessions is remembered better than one block.
Recalling information from memory, for example with a self-quiz.
The process that makes new memories more stable after learning.
The extra time and mistakes that come from switching between tasks.
Packing all your study into one long session just before a deadline.

trains.title: Memory, as a railway
lines: Think of memory as a railway network.
Encoding is laying new track. Storage is the track staying in place. Retrieval is running a train along it.
Lines that are used often stay clear. Lines that are not used get overgrown. This is forgetting.
Spacing is running a train every few days, so the line never gets fully overgrown.

football.title: Memory, as a football team
lines: Think of learning as practising a set piece.
Encoding is learning it in training. Storage is the team still knowing it next week. Retrieval is pulling it off in a match.
Practising it in match conditions works better than watching replays. This is retrieval practice.
Training a little every few days works better than one long session. This is the spacing effect.

references: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot. English translation: Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1913).
Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97.
Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.
Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
Sana, F., Weston, T., & Cepeda, N. J. (2013). Laptop multitasking hinders classroom learning for both users and nearby peers. Computers & Education, 62, 24–31.
